title: Your First Tournament
summary: What happens at a debate tournament, what to bring, how rounds are scheduled, and how to make the most of a long, fun day, whatever your record.

ol: **Registration**: your coach enters you ahead of time, usually on Tabroom.
**Pairings**: before each round, the tournament posts who you debate, which side you're on (or that there will be a coin flip), the room, and the judge.
**Preliminary rounds**: often four to six rounds, against different opponents, on both sides of the topic.
**Elimination rounds** ("outrounds"): the debaters with the best records advance; from here, each loss ends your tournament.
**Awards**: for the top teams and the top speakers (by speaker points).

list: Your cases for both sides, printed or on a laptop if your league allows it, and a backup copy.
Your evidence and answer files, organized so you can find anything in seconds.
Plenty of flow paper and pens in two colors.
A timer (a phone in airplane mode is fine where allowed; the [debate timer](/debate/tools/timer/) works offline once loaded).
Water, snacks, and something to do between rounds.
Dress as your league expects; many expect business clothes.
Find your room early. Introduce yourself to your opponents and judge.
Read your judge's paradigm if one is posted, and adapt (see [Judging and Ballots](/debate/learn/judging-and-ballots/)).
Set up your flows with the other side's likely arguments in mind.
Agree with your opponent on who keeps time if the judge doesn't.
Write down what arguments you heard and how you answered them, while it's fresh.
Fix one thing in your case if a judge's comment or a strong opponent exposed a hole.
Don't dwell on a loss. Every experienced debater has lost plenty of rounds; the next one starts fresh.
Watch a teammate's round if you have a free slot. You'll learn as much as from your own.

p: Your first tournament is for learning. Good goals are things you control: give every speech to the full time, answer every argument, ask three good cross-ex questions, weigh in every final speech. Wins follow skills, and most of the skills are built in rounds you lose.

practice: Hold a full practice round with the timer for the format you'll compete in, including prep time.
Make a one-page "frontline" of short answers to the three arguments you most expect.
Pack your tournament bag the night before using the list above.
